title: 1956 Scottish Airlines Malta air disaster
summary: A Scottish Airlines Avro York took off from Luqa Airport in Malta with 45 passengers and five crew. Shortly after becoming airborne, the boost enrichment capsule in the carburetor of engine one failed, and the engine caught fire. The pilots failed to feather the propeller, then after retracting flaps at low speed the aircraft entered a stall and unrecoverable dive, crashing near Żurrieq.
probable_cause: Engine failure followed by inappropriate crew response to low-speed stall, including nose-up control inputs that deepened the stall.

factors.evidence: The boost enrichment capsule in the carburetor of the number one engine failed, and the engine caught fire.
After retracting flaps at very low speed the aircraft went into a nose-up attitude, which resulted in a stall.
The aircraft stalled which caused it to enter an unrecoverable dive.
Aircraft entered an unrecoverable dive and crashed into the ground.

events.text: The Avro York, registration G-ANSY, took off from Luqa Airport, Malta at 12:21 UTC time with 45 passengers and five crew aboard.
Shortly after becoming airborne, the boost enrichment capsule in the carburetor of the number one engine failed, and the engine caught fire.
The pilots failed to feather the propeller as the aircraft slowly climbed to 700–800 feet; they then made a left turn to return to the airport.
Shortly after retracting the flaps, the aircraft went into a nose-up attitude at very low speed.
This resulted in a stall, which caused the aircraft to enter an unrecoverable dive and crash into the ground near the town of Żurrieq.

title: Linea Aeropostal Venezolana 253 (June 1956)

location.name: Atlantic Ocean off Asbury Park, New Jersey

summary: Flight 253 turned back to New York after Captain Plata reported the No. 2 propeller overspeeding and could not be feathered. While descending and dumping fuel off Asbury Park, escort crews saw the streaming fuel ignite near the No. 3 engine; the Super Constellation swerved, nosed over and plunged into the Atlantic, killing all 74 aboard. The board believed propeller vibration had damaged the wing near the fuel dump chute, providing the likely ignition source, but could not confirm it with certainty.
probable_cause: The board considered it most probable that vibration from the runaway No. 2 propeller damaged the wing structure near the fuel dump chute, providing the ignition source for the dumped fuel, though it could not determine this with certainty.

factors.evidence: Captain Plata reported the No. 2 propeller overspeeding and the crew declared an emergency, unable to feather it.
vibration induced by the runaway #2 propeller had caused internal structural damage to the starboard wing... between the fuel tank and fuel dump chute
the crews of both escort aircraft observed the streaming fuel catch fire and erupt in a large fireball
The airliner swerved violently to the right, nosed over, and plunged into the sea, exploding on impact

events.text: Captain Plata reported the No. 2 propeller, inboard on the port wing, was overspeeding, and radioed his intent to return to Idlewild.
The crew declared an emergency, stating they had been unable to feather the No. 2 propeller.
Captain Plata requested and received permission to dump fuel, and began doing so at 1:29.
The crews of both escort aircraft observed the streaming fuel catch fire near the No. 3 engine and erupt in a large fireball.
The airliner swerved violently to the right, nosed over, and plunged into the sea, exploding on impact 32 miles east of Asbury Park.

notes: Board could not confirm the ignition source with certainty; investigating agency not named.

title: 1956 Grand Canyon mid-air collision
summary: A TWA Constellation and United DC-7 collided over the Grand Canyon at 10:32 am in uncontrolled airspace. The two aircraft collided at an angle of about 25 degrees, and the DC-7's left wing clipped the Constellation's vertical stabilizer and fuselage, causing the tail assembly to break away. The Constellation entered a near-vertical terminal velocity dive and disintegrated on impact, while the DC-7 entered a rapidly descending left spiral and crashed into a cliff. All 128 people aboard both aircraft were killed.
probable_cause: The collision took place in uncontrolled airspace where it was the pilots' responsibility to maintain separation by 'see and be seen'. Investigation could not determine conclusively how much opportunity was available for the pilots to see and avoid each other due to uncertainty regarding high altitude visibility.

factors.evidence: At 10:32 am the two aircraft collided over the canyon at an angle of about 25 degrees.
It was not possible to determine conclusively how much opportunity was available for pilots to see and avoid each other.
There was uncertainty regarding high altitude visibility at the time of the collision.
The collision highlighted the antiquated state of air traffic control.

events.text: TWA Flight 2 departed Los Angeles at 9:01 am PST
United Air Lines Flight 718 departed Los Angeles at 9:04 am PST
Both aircraft in uncontrolled airspace, Constellation at 19000 ft and DC-7 at 21000 ft
The two aircraft collided over the canyon at an angle of about 25 degrees
The DC-7's left wing clipped the Constellation's vertical stabilizer and struck the fuselage, causing the tail assembly to break away
The separation of the tail assembly resulted in immediate loss of control, causing the aircraft to enter a near-vertical terminal velocity dive
The Constellation plunged into the Grand Canyon at an estimated speed of more than 700 ft/s and slammed into the north slope of Temple Butte and disintegrated on impact
The DC-7's left wing to the left of the number one engine was mangled and the crippled airliner entered a rapidly descending left spiral and collided with the south side cliff of Chuar Butte

title: 1956 Atlantic R6D-1 disappearance
summary: A Navy R6D-1 Liftmaster disappeared over the Atlantic Ocean about 590 kilometers southwest of Land's End, England, at approximately 22:10 on 10 October 1956 with the loss of all 59 people on board. The aircraft was on a scheduled Military Air Transport Service flight from RAF Lakenheath to Lajes Field in the Azores. A 14-day search found only wheels and a life raft floating in the ocean; no other trace of the aircraft or occupants was ever found.
probable_cause: The cause of the disappearance could not be determined. Only wheels and a life raft were recovered floating in the ocean. No trace of the crew or passengers was ever found.

factors.evidence: only wheels and a life raft floating 596 km southwest of Lands End; no trace of the aircraft
aircraft disappeared over the Atlantic Ocean

events.text: Aircraft carrying 9 crew and 50 passengers on scheduled flight from RAF Lakenheath to Lajes Field
Aircraft disappeared over the Atlantic Ocean about 590 kilometers southwest of Land's End; 14-day search found only wheels and a life raft

notes: Aircraft disappearance with no wreckage recovery; cause completely unknown; minimal information available

title: Linea Aeropostal Venezolana 253 (November 1956)
summary: Flight 253 was en route from New York to Caracas through a rainstorm approaching the destination airport. The pilot did not follow the approved semi-IFR procedure for entering Caracas, instead attempting a direct approach after accumulating navigation errors in speed estimation. The aircraft descended below safe altitude and struck the southern ridge of Cerro El Ávila at 6,700 feet, approximately 18 kilometers from the runway, killing all 25 passengers and crew.
probable_cause: The pilot did not comply with the approved instrument flight procedure and attempted a direct approach after accumulating navigation errors, resulting in insufficient altitude to safely cross the Ávila mountain range.

factors.evidence: The pilot-in-command did not fully comply with the approved procedure for entering Maiquetia in semi-IFR conditions and instead endeavoured to make a direct approach
After accumulating errors in estimating his speed, the pilot attempted the direct approach
His altitude at the time of his last report was insufficient to cross the Ávila mountain range
Flight 253 was flying through a rainstorm as it approached Caracas Airport
The aircraft struck the southern ridge of Cerro El Ávila at 6,700 feet
